rv.q: Old-fashioned though it may seem in contrast, in its density and epic ambition, its mixture of high-powered ideas and gut-wrenching emotions, it’s a show that feels lastingly revolutionary.
But it’s clear from this major retread that it still has bags of mileage – as does this gorgeously reborn Edwardian theatre.
But it also gives this play a relentlessness that manufactured moments of comedy or awkwardness don’t fully defray.

But seeing Les Mis for a second time was a chastening experience and one that reminded me that there are two things that audiences crave in the theatre and that are all too rarely found: an optimistic philosophy and a direct appeal to the heart.
The show remains grossly melodramatic, overlong and overloud.
The show remains a thrilling triumph.
I don’t think anybody could realistically see this imperfect, absurd, magnificent show and suggest that its crown as London’s longest-runner is in any danger.
It may not be revolutionary, but it gets everything right and delivers an unforgettable evening of musical theatre.
Les Misérables is one of the best musicals of all time and this new version will undoubtedly run for years.
At the end of the day, you can either hate the bombast of the music or thrill to its open-souled and self-sacrificing idealism.
It's a must see and I'm not surprised it's still delighting audiences.
